section.title: Prison Ships
section.p: Ms. Eagle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (1) what companies his Department has been in contact with regarding the proposal to moor prison ships in Birkenhead and Barrow;
(2) what timetable he is considering for the possible establishment of floating prisons;
(3) what is the estimated cost of hiring staffing and maintaining prison ships in the Wallasey or Birkenhead docks.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: Responsibility for this matter has been delegated to the director general of the prison service, who has been asked to arrange for a reply to be given.

p.i: Letter from Mr. D. Lewis to Ms Angela Eagle, dated 26 July 1993:
p.quote: The Home Secretary has asked me to reply to your recent Questions about prison ships.

Maritime detention facilities are one of the options being considered as part of a Prison Service contingency planning exercise. This exercise is intended to identify options for coping with levels of prisoner population that exceed the available accommodation. A number of sites with the necessary docking facilities are being reviewed, but no decision has been taken on the feasibility of this option.
As consideration of the option is at such an early stage, it is not possible to give the details of costs. Nor have there been any decisions on which companies could supply the accommodation.

As the contacts so far have been of a very preliminary nature and any decision to proceed with this option might involve a competitive tender, details of individual companies interested could not properly be revealed at this stage.

Mr. Maclean: Information on the amount of fines imposed at all courts following conviction under criminal law for the years 1986, 1989, 1990 and 1991 is given in the table. Comparable data for years prior to 1986 and for 1987 and 1988 are unavailable. It is not possible to identify fines separately from other similar receipts such as confiscation orders, forfeit bail sureties or magistrates' courts fees. All monies collected from magistrates' courts are surrendered direct to the Consolidated Fund and are not appropriated in aid of any vote.

section.title: Prisoners (Drugs)
section.p: Mr. Rathbone: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what plans he has to improve community care assessment arrangements for drug misusing prisoners remanded in custody or sentenced.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: Responsibility for this matter has been delegated to the Director General of the Prison Service, who has been asked to arrange for a reply to be given.

p.i: Letter from Mr. D. Lewis to Mr. Tim Rathbone, dated 26 July 1993:
p.quote: The Home Secretary has asked me to reply to your recent question about plans to improve community care assessment arrangements for drug misusing prisoners remanded in custody or sentenced.

The arrangements for assessment for community care for people in contact with the Criminal Justice System were published recently in Home Office Circular 29/1993. A copy of this Circular is enclosed, it is also available in the library. We are currently undertaking a review of services provided for drug misusers in prison with the aim of producing a comprehensive strategy to address drug misuse. Preparation for discharge and aftercare arrangements will be included in this review.

section.title: Electoral Registration
section.p: Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what measures he is taking in his review of electoral registration procedures to address the difficulties experienced by homeless people in registering to vote.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: As part of our post-election review, the electoral registration working group recently met representatives of the Church of England, the Salvation Army, Shelter and CHAR—the campaign for the homeless and rootless—to discuss the difficulties experienced by homeless people in registering as electors. We intend to hold further discussions later in the year.

section.title: Football Pools
section.p: Mr. Alton: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what representations he has received from Vernons Pools about the sale of pools coupons through retail outlets; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: The managing director of Vernons Pools wrote to me earlier this month about the timing of the commencement of clause 56 of the National Lottery Etc., Bill which will remove the prohibition on the use of premises for the delivery of football pools coupons and stakes. In order to ensure that the national lottery is not disadvantaged, we intend to defer the commencement of clause 56—and indeed of the other provisions of part IV of the Bill—until the launch of the lottery.

section.title: Wind Power
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make it his policy to commence a tendering process to construct a demonstration offshore wind farm.
Mr. Eggar: I have no plans to construct a demonstration offshore wind farm.

Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make it his policy to allow community-based wind power schemes to advertise for local investment; and if he will seek to place a statutory duty on local authorities to identify suitable sites for such developments.

Mr. Eggar: I am not aware of any impediment to community-based wind power schemes advertising for local investment. Planning Policy Guidance Note 22: Renewable Energy advises local authorities to include renewables in their development plan and provides guidance on how this should be done. It includes an annex on wind power.

Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade when he expects to make an announcement of when wind power developers can next apply for contracts under the non-fossil fuel obligation; and if he will make a statement concerning the procedure for the award of such contracts.
Mr. Eggar: I refer the hon. Member to my reply of 21 July to the hon. Member for Cambridgeshire, North-East (Mr. Moss), Official Report, column 339.
Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make it his policy that the next tranche of wind power contracts should be for not less than 700 MW.

Mr. Eggar: I currently expect to make the third renewable energy order under the non-fossil fuel obligation for approximately 300 to 400 MW of new capacity in total but will review this in light of the quality and cost of proposals received. I am considering a separate band for wind power within that total.

Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make it his policy to ensure that all contracts for renewable energy under the non-fossil fuel obligation are for a minimum of 10 years beginning from the date of commissioning the projects.

Mr. Eggar: My intention is that the third renewables order will run for 15 to 20 years as from November 1994. This will allow the public electricity suppliers to offer generators contracts for a similar period.

section.title: Energy from Waste
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what percentage of non-nuclear contracts granted under the non-fossil fuel obligation have been given to companies involved in the generation of energy through waste incineration in each year since 1987.

Mr. Eggar: Under the 1990 Non-Fossil Fuel Obligation Renewables Order, seven out of 75 renewables contracts went to waste incineration projects. Under the 1991 order 14 out of 122 contracts went to waste incineration projects.

(c): The contract prices awarded to projects under the 1990 order varied, and are commercially confidential. Under the 1991 order, waste incineration projects in the "Municipal and General Industrial Waste" band receive a premium of 6·55 p/kWh; while those in the "Other" band receive a premium of 5·9 p/kWh.
(d): The amount of electricity generated by all projects is commercially confidential.

section.title: Biogas and Hydroelectric Schemes
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what efforts are currently undertaken by his Department to encourage the development of biogas schemes and smaller hydroelectric schemes.

Mr. Eggar: My Department's renewable energy programme aims to stimulate the development of renewable sources of energy which have prospects of being economically competitive and environmentally acceptable. The non-fossil fuel obligation is stimulating an initial market. Biogas and small scale hydro are being supported under both the research programme and the non-fossil fuel obligation.

Mr. Eggar: (a) and (b): The names, locations and capacities of waste incineration projects which received contracts under the 1990 and 1991 non-fossil fuel obligation renewables orders are as follows:

Mr. Eggar: I refer the hon. Member to the document which I placed in the Libraries of both Houses giving details of the proposed arrangements of the third renewables order under the non-fossil fuel obligation, to which I referred in my reply of 21 July to the hon. Member for Cambridgeshire, North-East (Mr. Moss) Official Report, column 339. My intention is that the third order will run for 15 to 20 years as from November 1994, which will allow the public electricity suppliers to offer generators contracts for a similar period.

section.title: Nuclear Waste
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade, pursuant to the reply to the hon. Member for Pembroke (Mr. Ainger), Official Report, 20 July, column 126, what were the dates over which the vitrified high-level waste was delivered to Japan, the mode of transport used, the quantity involved and the location to which it was sent in Japan.
Mr. Eggar: The operational details are a matter for British Nuclear Fuels plc and its customer in Japan.
Mr. Dalyell: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what assessment has been made of Russian technical capacity to process nuclear waste.

Mr. Eggar [holding answer 8 July 1993]: British Nuclear Fuels plc is in discussion with the Russian Ministry of Atomic Power on the management of that country's nuclear waste. I understand that the parties have identified a number of areas in which collaboration between them can usefully take place and that they have agreed to meet on a regular basis.

Mrs. Mahon: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what progress has been made in conducting a study with BNFL on financial consequences of abandoning THORP, including the alternative use of already committed capital investment for the interim storage of contracted foreign spent fuel, as recommended in the First report of the Environment Committee of Session 1985–86, HC 191, on radioactive waste; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Eggar: The Government did not accept the recommendation in question.

Mr. Tipping: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what assurances overseas customers using the thermal oxide reprocessing plant have given that they will accept returns of high-level waste in accordance with the substitution principle; if Government approval of the principle will be conditional on such assurances; and what assessment he has made of the extent of facilities in recipient countries to provide adequate storage for such waste.

Mr. Eggar [holding answer 23 July 1993]: The Government's consideration of the proposal by British Nuclear Fuels plc to return nuclear waste by substitution has not yet been completed. Should substitution be approved, it would be for the company to negotiate appropriate arrangements with its customers within guidelines set by the Government. Customers who did not wish to accept substitution on a basis acceptable to the United Kingdom would be required to take delivery of all three waste streams—high, intermediate and low-level waste.

Mr. Tipping: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what information he has about the comparative costs of transporting intermediate-level waste arising from the reprocessing of foreign spent nuclear fuel at the thermal oxide reprocessing plant back to customer countries against storing the intermediate-level waste in the United Kingdom.
Mr. Eggar [holding answer 23 July 1993]: This is a commercial matter for British Nuclear Fuels plc and its overseas customers.

section.title: Atomic Energy Authority
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what progress has been made in meeting his target to ensure the first phase of work on options for the future of the AEA is completed by late autumn.

Mr. Eggar: The consultancy study I announced on 1 April, Official Report, column 407, is progressing to schedule. An announcement will be made in due course, once I have had an opportunity to consider the consultants' report and the AEA's own views.

section.title: Nuclear Safety (CIS)
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on the progress made in establishing a training seminar for nuclear safeguards experts from the Commonwealth of Independent States republics.

Mr. Eggar: In collaboration with BNFL and AEA my Department has to date arranged and funded three safeguards seminars for experts from the CIS Republics. Two of these were attended by personnel from the Russian Federation and concentrated on safeguards approaches for reprocessing plants, the third dealt with safeguards for fuel fabrication plants and fast reactors and included participants from the Republic of Kazakhstan in addition to the Russian Federation. A further two seminars are planned for the autumn.

section.title: Nuclear Industry
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade, pursuant to his answer of 19 July, Official Report, column 13, on what occasions in regard to what nuclear materials the European Commission has granted a derogation under article 22 of EC Regulation 3227/76 for nuclear exports from the United Kingdom.
Mr. Eggar: Derogation from reporting has been granted to the Science museum, South Kensington, London for uranium and thorium specimens.

Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what estimates he has of the surpluses expected to be generated by Nuclear Electric, Scottish Nuclear and British Nuclear Fuel's operations from 1993 to 1998; and what restrictions he intends to place on their use.

Mr. Eggar: The profitability of Nuclear Electric, Scottish Nuclear and BNFL over the period 1993–98 will depend on a number of factors, many of which are inevitably uncertain. In their role as shareholder, the Government undertake appropriate monitoring of the companies' expenditure plans.

Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what the increase in liabilities would be for British Nuclear Fuels, Scottish Nuclear and Nuclear Electric if discounting is not applied to nuclear provisions.
Mr. Eggar: These are matters for the companies concerned.

Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what research has been undertaken to verify that the two per cent. discount rate applied to nuclear liabilities by United Kingdom nuclear companies correctly balances the risks and benefits between current and future generations.
Mr. Eggar: This is a matter for the nuclear companies.

Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on progress in making his target in implementation of extended reporting of nuclear materials and equipment by August 1993.
Mr. Eggar: The submission of confidential returns has begun.

section.title: Nuclear Emergencies
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what progress has been made in his target to develop by August a strategy for use of the radioactive incident monitoring network in a United Kingdom emergency through integration into the existing nuclear emergency briefing room procedures.

Mr. Eggar: Radioactive incident monitoring network equipment has been installed within the nuclear emergency briefing room and Department of Trade and Industry staff have participated in testing and demonstration of the system. Agreement has been reached in general terms on how it will be integrated into nuclear emergency briefing room procedures when the radioactive incident monitoring network phase 2 comes on stream towards the end of this year.

section.title: Advanced Gas-cooled Reactor Fuel
section.p: Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what discussions his Department has had with (a) British Nuclear Fuels Limited, (b) Costain Engineering or (c) Nuclear Electric regarding plans on construction of a dry store for spent advanced gas-cooled reactor fuel.
Mr. Eggar: My Department discusses a range of topics with these companies.

section.title: Thermal Oxide Reprocessing Plant
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what response he has made to the letter sent to the Minister for Energy on 5 July by the chairman of the Consumers Union of Japan relating to THORP.
Mr. Eggar: The letter arrived on 19 July. I shall be replying in due course.
Mr. Colvin: To ask the President of the Board of Trade when he expects THORP to be commissioned; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Eggar: Before commissioning its thermal oxide reprocessing plant, British Nuclear Fuels plc will need such consents and authorisations as may be required by law. As my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for the Environment announced on 28 June, Official Report, column 392, there is to be a further round of consultation. This is expected to start shortly and to last for two months. Final decisions will be taken following this further period of consultation.

section.title: Uranium
section.p: Mr. Martyn Jones: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what was the price per tonne of uranium in 1977, adjusted to 1993 prices; what was the projected price for 1993 given in the Windscale inquiry report; what is the current cost per tonne of uranium; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Eggar: The Euratom Supply Agency's report for 1992 shows that the average price of natural uranium deliveries made during the year under multiannual contracts to the electricity utilities of the European Community or their procurement organisations was 49·50 ecu per kilogramme of uranium. The agency's 1977 646 report did not provide a comparable figure for that year because of uncertain conditions in the market. Illustrative prices for uranium were mentioned in chapter 9 of the Windscale inquiry report.

Mr. Martyn Jones: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how much uranium separated by reprocessing at Sellafield over the last 40 years has been used in reactors (a) by weight and (b) as percentage of total uranium produced.
Mr. Eggar: I refer the hon. Member to my reply to the hon. Member for Clydesdale (Mr. Hood) on 20 July 1993, Official Report, columns 127–28.

section.title: Environmentally Friendly Fuel Technology
section.p: Mr. Robathan: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what action has been taken following the representations the former Department of Energy received from the Director General of Electricity Supply about the inclusion of environmentally friendly technologies, including such as combined heat and power, in the non-fossil fuel obligation; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Eggar: I understand that the then Secretary of State for Energy took full account of his consultations with the Director General of Electricity Supply when making the 1990 and 1991 renewables orders under the non-fossil fuel obligation. Both orders are supporting projects with the potential for combined heat and power. On 21 July I announced a third renewables order under the non-fossil fuel obligation. I would expect projects with the potential for combined heat and power to bid into this order also.

section.title: Oil Exploration
section.p: Mr. Harvey: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how the environmental interests of the coast are safeguarded during the oil exploration licensing procedure.

Mr. Eggar: The Department of Trade and Industry consults other Government Departments, the joint Nature Conservation Committee and local advisory groups before offering any blocks for licensing. The JNCC in turn consults English Nature, the Countryside Council for Wales, Scottish Natural Heritage and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds.

Blocks that are offered for licensing in sensitive areas such as those close to the coast are subject to special conditions to protect wildlife and the environment. These conditions are agreed with relevant Government Departments and the JNCC.

The conditions include consultation with JNCC and other environmental organisations before the licensee undertakes operations; seasonal restrictions to protect wildlife; a ban on drilling within three miles of the coast; the use of zero-discharge rigs and water-based drilling muds; and to agree with the advisory bodies and local authorities plans to be put into effect in case of an oil spill.

section.title: Depleted Uranium
section.p: Mrs. Anne Campbell: To ask the President of the Board of Trade to which foreign defence industries the British nuclear industry supplies depleted uranium.

Mr. Eggar: All shipments of depleted uranium are made in accordance with the provisions of the Export of Goods (Control) Order 1992. It has been the policy of successive Administrations not to make public the details of specific export licence applications. In assessing all such applications the Government take into account the United Kingdom's obligations under the nuclear non-proliferation treaty.

section.title: Renewable Energy
section.p: Mr. Harvey: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what publicly financed grants are available to scientists and entrepreneurs for research into and development of renewable energy technology.

Mr. Eggar: My Department operates a research and development programme on renewable energy. Financial assistance may be available to appropriate projects. Interested parties should contact:
Enquiry Bureau
Energy Technology Support
Harwell Laboratory
Oxfordshire
OX11 ORA

section.title: Pharmaceuticals
section.p: Mr. Cousins: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what was the volume and value of exports of anthrax vaccine in each year since 1985

Mr. Needham: The information requested is not available from official sources because the United Kingdom trade classification does not separately identify anthrax vaccines. The manufacturers of anthrax vaccines in the United Kingdom report no exports during the last five years. Information prior to that could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: KONVER Programme
section.p: Dr. David Clark: To ask the President of the Board of Trade, pursuant to his answer to the hon. Member for Barrow and Furness (Mr. Hutton), of 14 June, Official Report, columns 409–10, which bodies have been consulted for their views on the draft United Kingdom programme for the KONVER scheme; and what is the planned size of the draft United Kingdom programme.
Mr. Sainsbury [holding answwer 23 July 1993]: The United Kingdom KONVER programme will request 20·12 million ecu, which is the full amount allocated to the United Kingdom for 1993.

Consultation on the draft programme will proceed during August, and will include the training and enterprise councils, the local enterprise companies, the local authority associations, and the Rural Development Commission.

section.title: Blind and Partially Sighted People
section.p: Mr. Matthew Taylor: To ask the President of the Board of Trade (1) what arrangements his Department makes to ensure that blind and partially sighted people have access to information produced by his Department where it has not been published in alternative media such as Braille, large print or tape;
(2) what is his Department's policy on which information produced by his Department is published in alternative media to standard print such as Braille, tape or large print.

Mr. Eggar: The Department's information materials are freely available. We are not aware of widespread demand for them to be separately prepared for blind and partially sighted people, but the need for such provision is kept under review.

section.title: Contracting Out
section.p: Mr. McAllion: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will list all those services or functions contracted out in his Department and agencies, since November 1991, in which the Transfer or Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981 were not applied.

Mr. Eggar: In my Department no services or functions have been contracted out where the Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations were relevant. Collection of information on all contracts where TUPE was not applicable would incur disproportionate costs.

section.title: Data Processing
section.p: Mr. McAllion: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will list the numbers of staff by grade that are employed in his Department and agencies in the automatic data processing functional specialism.

Mr. Eggar: The Department and its agencies employ the following staff in the automatic data processing functional specialism:
Number
Senior Executive Officer 61
Higher Executive Officer 136
Executive Officer 156

section.title: Computer Consultants
section.p: Mr. McAllion: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will list all the computer consultancies employed by his Department and agencies, since November 1991, the tasks for which they were engaged, and the total cost to his Department.
Mr. Eggar: My Department does not classify consultancies in terms of their activity and collection of this information would incur disproportionate costs.

section.title: Zinc
section.p: Mr. Nicholas Winterton: To ask the President of the Board of Trade (1) what recent representations he has received concerning distortions in the world trade in zinc ash and residue, zinc dross, unwrought zinc, and zinc waste and scrap; and if he will make a statement;
(3) what steps he is taking to bring about free and fair trade in zinc ash and residue, zinc dross, unwrought zinc, and zinc waste and scrap;

(4) what information he has concerning the net balance of trade in terms of volume and value between the United Kingdom and India in zinc ash and residue, zinc dross, unwrought zinc, and zinc waste and scrap.
Mr. Sainsbury: I will write to my hon. Friend as soon as possible.

section.title: Defence Industry (Reduction)
section.p: Mrs. Ann Winterton: To ask the President of the Board of Trade (1) what steps he is taking to ensure that assistance from the European Community can be targeted to those communities which have suffered directly the greatest impact of reduced demand in the level of defence procurement regardless of whether or not they have assisted area status or are suffering overall regional or industrial decline;

(2) if he will make a statement providing details of the European Community KONVER programme for assistance to areas affected by reduced demand in the defence industries; whether assistance through this programme is available only to projects in locations with assisted area status or is more widely available; and what steps he is taking to ensure that the north west of England benefits from this programme.

Mr. Sainsbury [holding answers 13 July 1993]: Those areas which are within an objective 2 area will be eligible for assistance for activities supported by the European regional development fund within the KONVER scheme.

Moreover the conclusions reached at the Foreign Affairs Council on 2 and 3 July on the regulations on the future of European structural funds, confirmed by the Council on 19 and 20 July, enable member states to make available to areas not designated for objective 1, 2 or 5b a limited part of the European regional development fund contribution to KONVER. The Government intend to make use of this new flexibility in the United Kingdom's 1993 KONVER programme.
All areas affected by the reduction in defence expenditure will be eligible for support under the European social fund part of the scheme.
Eligibility for the structural funds is not affected by assisted area status.

section.title: Plutonium
section.p: Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how the value and cost of plutonium owned by United Kingdom nuclear companies is treated for accounting purposes.
Mr. Eggar: This is a commercial matter for the companies concerned.

section.title: Consultancy Contracts
section.p: Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what use he intends to make of consultants in the forthcoming nuclear review; and what safeguards he intends to institute in respect of auditors of companies in 650 the nuclear industry who tender for consultancy contracts associated with the review to ensure no conflict of interest occurs.
Mr. Eggar: No decisions have yet been taken on the scope, timing and format of the nuclear review, or on whether consultants will be employed. A further announcement will be made in due course.

section.title: Unemployment
section.p: Mr. Pope: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what steps he is taking to assist areas with rising unemployment, in particular areas of high concentrations of defence-related industry; what special programmes are available for such areas; and what plans he has to increase such assistance.

Mr. Redwood: The assisted area review took into account future rundowns, including those arising from reductions in defence expenditure. As a result the Haverfordwest and Fishguard travel-to-work areas have been upgraded to development area status to assist further in the work taken forward through the west Wales task force.

section.title: Youth Organisations
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will list the national voluntary youth organisations within Wales currently in receipt of funding from his Department, indicating when each organisation was informed of their grant levels for the current year.

Sir Wyn Roberts: There are 15 youth organisations currently in receipt of grant, namely the Boys Brigade, Baptist Youth Ministry, Church in Wales, Guides Cymru, Gwerin y Coed (Woodcraft Folk), the Order of St. John, Phab (Wales), United Nations Association International Youth Services, United Reform Church, Urdd Gobaith Cymru, Wales Federation of Young Farmers' Clubs, Welsh Association of Youth Clubs, Welsh Federation of Boys' and Girls' Groups, Welsh Scout Council, and the Young Men's Christian Association of Wales.
All organisations were informed of their grant levels for 1993–94 on 8 April, except the Welsh Association of Youth Clubs, which was informed on 26 May as its application was handled separately.

section.title: Wales Youth Agency
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) if he will list the training materials produced to date by the Wales Youth Agency aimed at (a) young people and (b) those employed in the youth service since the establishment of the agency;
(2) if he will list the publicity leaflets aimed at young people produced by the Wales Youth Agency since its establishment;

(3) how many consultation exercises have been undertaken to date by the Wales Youth Agency with organisations of young people; and if he will list (a) the subject of each consultation and (b) the organisations which were consulted.
Sir Wyn Roberts: This information is not held centrally.

Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will make it his policy to investigate staffing decisions undertaken by the Wales Youth Agency in relation to former employees of the Welsh Youth Forum.
Sir Wyn Roberts: No. The Department has been kept informed of the agency's staffing decisions relating to former employees of the Wales Youth Forum.

Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) what representations have been received by his Department from the Wales Youth Agency since its establishment concerning (a) the participation of young people in decision making and (b) the future of the youth service agency;
(2) if he will list the written representation received by his Department from the Wales Youth Agency since its establishment on policy issues affecting young people.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The Wales Youth Agency has made representations on the future of the Welsh youth card, information needs of young people, young people's membership of the management board: youth service funding, innovatory grants scheme in Wales, and the validation of training for youth workers in Wales.

Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will list the meetings held to date between members of his Department and members of the Wales Youth Agency, indicating the date and purpose of each meeting.
Sir Wyn Roberts: Since its establishment in April 1992, the Department has met the chairman, vice-chairman and other members of the Wales Youth Agency's management board on three occasions.

tr.td: Introductory meeting with chairman and vice-chairman and vice-chairman

section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will list the members on the management group of the Wales Youth Agency, indicating their names and representative organisations; and which members are aged 25 years or under.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The management board's membership is:
Name Representative body
Mr. Gerald Davies (Chairman) Personal capacity

Mrs. Beverly Martin Personal capacity
Mr. Brian Thirsk Wales Association of Full-time Youth and Community Workers

section.title: Youth Service
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what plans he has to introduce a statutory youth service in Wales and to develop a formula for funding local youth service provision.

Sir Wyn Roberts: None. Local education authorities already have a statutory duty to secure provision for their areas of adequate facilities for further education, and for recreation, social and physical training for those of school age. These provisions cover the youth service.

The resources made available to Welsh local authorities through the annual local authority revenue settlement are not attributed to particular services. Youth service funding at the local level is a matter for individual authorities to determine in the light of local needs and priorities.

section.title: European Environmental Agency
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will make representations to the European Community advocating Wales as a location for the new European Environmental Agency.
Mr. Redwood: I refer the hon. Gentleman to the reply given to him on this issue on 24 February at column 634.

section.title: Aggregates
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will publish figures showing the estimated level of primary aggregates production in Wales by county (a) for the 1992–96 period and (b) between 2006–11; and what the 2006–11 production levels will be and the percentage of the 1992–96 levels in each instance.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: The Government do not provide guidance on primary aggregates production on a county basis. Details of the regional position based on the proposals in the draft revision of minerals planning guidance note 6, published in January, are available in the Library of the House.

section.title: Housing
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will list the Welsh housing authorities making non-statutory rate fund contributions to their housing revenue account in 1992–93, giving the amounts in each case.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: Council housing authorities can make contributions to the housing revenue account only in accordance with schedule 4 to the Local Government and Housing Act 1989 as amended by the Leasehold Reform Housing and Urban Development Act 1993.

section.title: Homelessness
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many bed-and-breakfast establishments are currently used by each local authority in Wales to house homeless people; and how many establishments have no (a) kitchen and (b) bathroom facilities.
Mr. Gwilym Jones: The information is not available centrally.

section.title: Youth Training
section.p: Ms Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) if he will list for each training and enterprise council in Wales their youth training performance in 1992–93 showing (a) the cost per output point and (b) the number of national vocational qualifications per 100 leavers, together with the latest information he has for 1993–94; and if he will make a statement;

(2) if he will list for each training and enterprise council in Wales their employment training performance in 1992–93 showing (a) the cost per output point, (b) the number of national vocational qualifications per 100 leavers and (c) the number of positive outcomes per 100 leavers, together with the latest information he has for 1993–94; and if he will make a statement.

Sir Wyn Roberts: Information on the performance of TECs in Wales in these areas is used for management purposes by my officials in their discussions with TECs. My approach to performance measurement is being refined and I will consider publishing comparative information in due course.

section.title: Woodlands
section.p: Mr. Richards: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what percentage of the total land mass of Wales is made of publicly-owned woodland and forests.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The publicly-owned forests and woodlands managed by the Forestry Commission cover about 6 per cent. of the total land area of Wales. Information on the area of woodland owned by other public bodies is not readily available but it is not thought that it would be significant as a percentage of the total land area.

Mr. Richards: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what measures are being taken to ensure the Welsh public will continue to have access to publicly-owned woodland; and if he will make a statement.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The Forestry Commission encourages people to enjoy the publicly-owned forests in its care through a "freedom to roam" policy. It also provides a range of visitor facilities, and caters for many outdoor activities and sports. The Commission will be continuing to implement these policies in its management of forests in the future.

Arrangements for securing continued public access to Forestry Commission woodlands sold under the disposals programme, by means of prior agreements entered into between the commission and local authorities, were introduced in October 1991. These arrangements will be reviewed this year in consultation with the countryside agencies and the local authority associations.
Mr. Richards: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many acres of woodland in Wales are open for public access; and if he will make a statement.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The Forestry Commission manages 127,000 hectares (about 315,000 acres) of woodland in Wales and encourages public access through a "freedom to roam" policy. Public access is also often permitted in woodlands under the management of local authorities and bodies such as the Woodland Trust, but figures for these and the areas of privately owned woodlands open to the public are not readily available.

section.title: Training and Enterprise Councils
section.p: Mr. Richards: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what measures are being taken in Wales to help those people graduating from TECs to find employment; and if he will make a statement.

Sir Wyn Roberts: All TEC training programmes are focused on obtaining employment through improved skills and qualifications. Trainees are provided with job search advice and support and TEC training providers maintain close contact with local employers. In addition the Employment Service provides a range of advisory and guidance services through its network of local offices.

The latest information available for 1992–93 indicates that following their period of training with TECs, 3,466 adult trainees and 5,309 youth trainees in Wales secured employment or progressed into further education or training.

section.title: Child Sex Abuse
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what level of funding has been granted by his Department to local authorities in Wales towards the development of specialist therapeutic and support services for sexually abused childen and their families in each of the last three years.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: Local authority social services expenditure is funded through the annual local authority revenue and capital settlements. It is for individual authorities to decide how to apportion those resources between and within services in accordance with their statutory obligations and their own priorities.

section.title: Secondary Schools
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many pupils attended each of the secondary schools in Wales in the school year 1992–93.

section.title: Pupil Exclusions
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will publish figures showing the number of pupil exclusions in (a) the primary sector and (b) the secondary school sector within each local education authority in Wales in each year since 1987; and what has been the percentage of excluded pupils within the general school population in each area in each year.
Sir Wyn Roberts: The information requested is not collected centrally.

section.title: School Books
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what was the expenditure per pupil on school books in each of the local education authorities in Wales in (a) the primary sector and (b) the secondary sector in each year since 1986 at constant prices.
Sir Wyn Roberts: The following tables give expenditure per pupil at constant prices on text and library books, and educational equipment, for the years requested.

section.title: Psychiatric Admissions
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many psychiatric admissions of children of 16 years or under have occurred within each health authority area in Wales in each of the last three years; and how many were diagnosed under conduct disorder in each instance.

tr.td: 1Includes neurotic, personality and other non-psychotic mental disorders.

section.p: Note: There are no Mental Illness Hospitals or units in Pembrokeshire.

section.title: GP Fund Holders
section.p: Mr. Gareth Wardell: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will publish for each fund-holding general medical practitioner's practice in Wales the per capita allocations for the purchase of hospital services in 1993–94.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: It would be inappropriate to publish per capita allocations for each fund-holding practice in Wales. Allocations reflect the individual nature and extent of these services with which patients in each practice have been provided over previous years. The per capita allocations to fund holders for the purchase of hospital services in 1993–94 on average amount to £71 per patient, and range from £44 to £128.
Mr. Gwilym Jones: The information given in the following table relates to children aged 16 or under admitted to mental illness hospitals and units in each health authority area.

section.title: Low Pay
section.p: Mr. Ron Davies: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what was the average wage of the lowest paid decile of the population in Wales in 1991 (a) at 1991 prices and (b) at 1979 prices.

Mr. Redwood: It is not statistical custom to calculate average earnings within the lowest or highest deciles. The New Earnings Survey estimates that, in 1991, 10 per cent. of full-time adult employees in Wales earned below £128·70 per week. At constant 1979 prices, the figure was £52·50 per week.

Mr. Redwood: The information requested is set out in the table.

section.title: Welshpool Bypass
section.p: Mr. Alex Carlile: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many accidents have occurred on the Welshpool bypass since its opening on 16 July; and if he will make a statement.

Sir Wyn Roberts: I am advised that up to 21 July, four accidents have been recorded by Dyfed/Powys police on the bypass or at its junctions. From an initial examination, it does not appear that the design of the new road has contributed to the incidents. The situation will be kept under close review.

Mr. Alex Carlile: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will instruct his highways department to re-design the Sarnybryncaled junctions on the Welshpool bypass; and if he will make a statement.

Sir Wyn Roberts: This junction has been designed in accordance with national standards. As is usual in the period after the opening of a new stretch of trunk road, use of the bypass will be closely monitored and any necessary improvements identified at Sarnybryncaled or elsewhere will be introduced.

section.title: Training

(4) if he will publish tables showing the latest available results from the youth training leavers survey for each training and enterprise council area in England and Wales and each local enterprise company in Scotland broken down to show the number and proportion of youth training leavers who were (a) in full-time work with the same employer, (b) in full-time work with a different employer, (c) in part-time work, (d) on a full-time course at a college or training centre, (e) on another youth training scheme, (f) doing something else, (g) who were unemployed, (h) who had obtained a vocational qualification, (i) the number of questionnaires issued, (j) the usable percentage response rate and (k) the percentage of respondents who were early leavers;

(6) if he will list for each region and for Great Britain as a whole the latest available information he has on the characteristics of those who have entered employment training showing (a) the number of entrants covered, (b) whether male or female, (c) duration of unemployment, (d) ethnic origin and (e) if they have a disability;

section.title: Child Care
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what action has been taken by his Department to implement the 1992 European Community recommendation on child care.

Miss Widdecombe: The Government welcome the recommendation, which is in tune with our policy of encouraging measures which allow parents to balance their work and family responsibilities. Since the recommendation was adopted in March 1992, we have introduced a major £45 million initiative to provide 50,000 extra out-of-school child care places for the over-fives. Shortly before the recommendation was adopted, we published the booklet, "The Best of Both Worlds" which illustrates with case studies a variety of flexible employment practices which can benefit working parents and employers alike. My right hon. Friend, the Secretary of State, in his previous post as the Secretary of State for Wales, launched the Chwarae Teg or "Fair Play" initiative which brings together a partnership of the public, private and voluntary sectors to promote new child care provision and flexible working as part of a strategy to increase opportunities for women in the work force. We will continue to look for opportunities to promote a more family-friendly working environment.

section.title: Restart
section.p: Ms Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment how many people in each region and Great Britain as a whole how many people attended a Restart interview in 1992–93 and in the first quarter of 1993–94; and what were the results of those interviews broken down in the same way as the reply given on 18 December 1990, Official Report, column 148.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: Responsibility for the subject of the question has been delegated to the Employment Service agency under its chief executive. I have asked him to arrange for a reply to be given.

p.i: Letter from M. E. G. Fogden to Ms Clare Short, dated 26 July 1993:
p.quote: As the Employment Service is an Executive Agency, the Secretary of State has asked me to write to you direct to respond to your Parliamentary Questions to him about how many people, for each region and for Great Britain as a whole, attended a Restart interview in 1992–93 and in the first 678 quarter of 1993–94; and what were the results of those interviews broken down in the same way as the reply given in the Official Report, column 148, on 18 December 1990. This is something which falls within the responsibilities delegated to me as Chief Executive of the Agency.

The Restart interview programme provides a framework within which the Employment Service provides help for long-term unemployed people. It provides a gateway to the range of employment and training opportunities available as well as being a means of ensuring that claimants remain available for and are actively seeking work.

During the 1992–93 operational year 2·8 million interviews were conducted and from these interviews 33,300 started work, 78,200 began training under Employment Training, 106,000 started in Jobclub, 112,100 started a Restart course and 6,900 started the Enterprise Allowance Scheme.

The Employment Service has changed its performance monitoring at a national level for 1993–94 and the information for this year cannot be given in exactly the same format as that previously provided. Information is not yet available for the first quarter of this operational year, the figures quoted are for the first two months. During the first two months of 1993–94 54,500 interviews were conducted and from these interviews 5,800 people started work and 95,600 started an Employment Department programme, such as Jobclub, Restart Course, Jobplan Workshop and Training For Work.

These figures reflect only the direct results of Restart. We do not know how many people subsequently take up a job or a place on an employment or training programme as a result of the guidance given to them at their interview.

An indication of the scale of that effect is provided by the report "The Restart Effect" which was recently published by the independent Policy Studies Institute. It is based on an analysis of the largest survey of unemployed people in the United Kingdom since 1980. This showed conclusively that the programme had a major effect in reducing the time it takes people to leave unemployment, to get a job and to enter Employment Training, particularly for those people who were at a disadvantage within the labour market.
I hope that this is helpful.

section.p: As decided by the Administration Committee of the House of Commons, Chief Executive replies to written Parliamentary Questions will now be published in the Official Report. I will also place a copy of this letter in the Library of the House.

section.title: Training and Enterprise Councils
section.p: Ms Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment how many training and enterprise council chairmen have left each TEC board since its launch; and how many TEC directors have resigned since the launch of their TEC.
Miss Widdecombe: A total of 34 training and enterprise council chairmen have left TEC boards since their launch.

A total of 328 TEC directors have left TEC boards since the launch of their TEC. This is principally due to changes in their business commitments, and reflects similar levels of turnover in the private sector as a whole.

Ms Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what is the latest available information on the number of male and female directors of training and enterprise councils; how many are from (a) ethnic minority backgrounds and (b) the private sector; what is the best information he has about which industrial sectors they come from; and how many of the non-private sector directors are from (i) local authorities, (ii) local education authorities, (iii) other educational organisations, (iv) trade unions, (v) voluntary organisations, (iv) ethnic minority organisations, (vii) employers' associations and (viii) others.
Miss Widdecombe: There are currently 942 male and 127 female directors of training and enterprise councils in England. Of these, 757 come from the private sector.

Information on the ethnic origin of TEC board members is provided voluntarily. The most up-to-date figures are from 1992 and cover only 44 TECs. Twenty board members are quoted as being of ethnic minority origin.
The Department does not maintain statistics on the industrial sector origins of private sector TEC directors.

Mr. William O'Brien: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will direct training and enterprise councils to publish annual statements of accounts for public inspection; and if he will make a statement.
Miss Widdecombe: Training and enterprise councils are required to publish an annual report and audited statement of accounts within four months after the relevant financial year.

Mr. William O'Brien: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what arrangements apply to the payment of salaries and other expenses of officers of local authorities who serve on boards of training and enterprise councils; and if he will make a statement.

Miss Widdecombe: Directors serving on boards of training and enterprise councils are refunded expenses reasonably incurred in connection with their duties on behalf of TECs. They are not renummerated.

Mr. William O'Brien: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will arrange for training and enterprise councils to provide information on individual local projects, including costs, on request by a member of the public or a district council; and if he will make a statement.

Miss Widdecombe: Training and enterprise councils are required to publish a summary of their corporate and business plans and annual reports. This is available to the public on request. TECs' corporate plans must also be made available for inspection by the public.
TECs are private companies. It is for them to determine what information they publish about the funding of specific projects.

section.title: Parental and Family Leave
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will make it his policy to support European Community directives on parental and family leave for employees.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: No.

section.title: Methyl Bromide
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will make representations to the European Community advocating the adoption of measures to protect workers from exposure to methyl bromide.

Mr. Michael Forsyth: A proposal for an EC directive on the protection of workers from chemical agents, such as methyl bromide, has recently been published. A comprehensive set of legislation already exists in the United Kingdom to protect workers from hazardous substances, including methyl bromide. The United Kingdom will press for the principles of this legislation to be incorporated in any corresponding Community measure.
Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what guidance is issued by his Department regarding protection of workers handling methyl bromide.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: In 1991, the Health and Safety Executive published guidance note CS 12: "Fumigation using methyl bromide (bromomethane)".

Additional guidance is available in the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 1988—COSHH—and the Control of Pesticides Regulations 1986. This includes an approved code of practice which gives practical guidance on the requirements of COSHH in relation to fumigation operations.

section.title: St. Helena (Work Permits)
section.p: Dr. Marek: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment how many work permits have been issued to citizens of St. Helena for each of the last 15 years; and what proposals he has for numbers in future years.

Miss Widdecombe: The number of work permits issued to citizens of St. Helena for each of the years for which figures are available is as follows:
681
Number
1986 20
1987 30
1988 28
1989 51
1990 53
1991 30
1992 34

There is no specific number of work permits planned to be issued to St. Helenians in future years. However, the maximum number of permits available to St. Helenians under the special dependent territories quota scheme is 35 in 1993 and 30 in 1994, when the scheme ends.
Applications for work permits for St. Helenians outside these arrangements will continue to be considered against the normal work permit scheme criteria.

section.title: ES Guide 39
section.p: Mr. Spellar: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment when ES guide 39 was issued; what it replaced; whether the letters in appendix V4 and appendix V3 were in the previous guide; and whether the note of guidance in clauses V 16 and V17 was in the previous guide.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: Responsibility for the subject of the question has been delegated to the Employment Service agency under its chief executive. I have asked him to arrange for a reply to be given.

p.i: Letter from M. E. G. Fogden to Mr. John Spellar, dated 26 July 1993:
p.quote: As the Employment Service is an Executive Agency, the Secretary of State has asked me to write to you direct to respond to your Parliamentary Question to him about ES Guide 39. This is something which falls within the responsibilities delegated to me as Chief executive of the Agency.

ES Guide 39 was issued in January 1993 and replaced the New Client Adviser Guide and the Claimant Adviser Handbook. The guidance contained in Section V paragraphs V16 and V17, and the letters in Appendices V3 and V4, have been taken directly from the Claimant Adviser Handbook. I enclose copies of the guidance previously contained in the Claimant Adviser Handbook and that in ES Guide 39 for your information.
I hope this is helpful.

section.p: As decided by the Administration Committee of the House of Commons, Chief Executive replies to written Parliamentary Questions will now be published in the Official Report. I will also place a copy of this letter in the Library of the House.

It must be made clear to the claimant that they are seeking their doctor's advice on their own behalf and not on behalf of the claimant adviser or the Employment Service.

section.p: Claimant Adviser Service
The Employment Service
Employment Department
Date

I am the claimant Adviser at……… benefit office; part of the Employment Service. I give advice to unemployed people to help them find suitable work and provide information about the benefits which they may receive. I also have to ensure that people satisfy the conditions of entitlement for receiving Unemployment Benefit, Income Support and/or credits of NI. One of the main conditions laid down in the Social Security Act 1975 is that the client must be capable of taking up suitable work.

When I interviewed your patient on………*he/she informed me that they had health problems that prevents them undertaking any employment. In these circumstances I have had to suggest that *he/she should seek your advice about their fitness for employment.
If in your opinion *he/she is incapable of all work then you will no doubt advise your patient in accordance with your own clinical judgement.

Should you advise your patient that *he/she is capable of work then it will be necessary for them to see me again to reconsider their claim to unemployment benefit, income support and/or credits of NI.
